Brazil. The largest country in South America by both area and population, occupying nearly half the continent's landmass. A former Portuguese colony from 1500 to 1822, it uniquely speaks Portuguese and absorbed millions of African slaves, creating a distinctive Afro-Portuguese culture. Its dominance of the Amazon rainforest, vast natural resources, and cultural influence make it a regional and global power.

The Amazon rainforest covers roughly sixty percent of the forest's total area. Brazil's sovereignty over this territory is simultaneously an ecological and geopolitical issue. Colonized by Portugal starting in 1500, Brazil developed as a sugar-producing colony dependent on enslaved labor, unlike Spanish America's emphasis on mining. Brazil received roughly forty-six percent of all African slaves transported across the Atlantic, more than four point nine million individuals, shaping Brazilian demographics, culture, language, and social inequality.

Brazil declared independence in 1822 under Pedro I. Unlike Spanish American republics, Brazil retained its monarchy until 1889, creating a unique political trajectory. The Atlantic rainforest on its eastern seaboard is a distinct, highly biodiverse, and severely endangered ecosystem separate from the Amazon. Carnival, rooted in Portuguese Catholic tradition and Afro-Brazilian culture, is among the world's largest festivals, held annually in Rio de Janeiro and other cities.

Modern Brazil is a middle power with significant soft power through football, music, and culture. Economic dependence on commodity exports including soybeans and iron ore creates vulnerability.
